We define a model in terms of a loss function ℒ \mathcal{L} with parameters θ \theta as a sum over training examples ( z i ) i = 1 n (z_{i})_{i=1}^{n} , i.e., ℒ ⁡ ( θ ) = ∑ i n ℓ ⁡ ( z i , θ ) \mathcal{L}(\theta)=\sum_{i}^{n}\ell(z_{i},\theta) , where ℓ \ell is an example-wise loss (e.g., mean-squared error or cross entropy). Let θ ⋆ \theta^{\star} be the parameters of the trained model, obtained by, e.g., minimizing the loss over this dataset, i.e., θ ⋆ = arg ​ min θ ⁡ ℒ ​ ( θ ) \theta^{\star}=\argmin_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta) . We write the prediction function given by parameters θ \theta at an input x x as y ^ ​ ( x , θ ) \hat{y}(x,\theta) . We consider the problem of auditing a trained model, where unlabeled test points x ′ x^{\prime} arrive one at a time in a stream, and we wish to assess underspecification on a point-by-point basis.

In this section, we introduce our local ensemble underspecification score ℰ m ​ ( x ′ ) \mathcal{E}_{m}(x^{\prime}) for an unlabeled test point x ′ x^{\prime} (significance of m m explained below). The score is designed to measure the variability that would be induced by randomly choosing predictions from an ensemble of models with similar training loss. Our score has a simple form: it is the norm of the prediction gradient g θ ⋆ ​ ( x ′ ) := ∇ θ y ^ ​ ( x ′ , θ ⋆ ) g_{\theta^{\star}}(x^{\prime}):=\nabla_{\theta}\hat{y}(x^{\prime},\theta^{\star}) multiplied by a matrix of Hessian eigenvectors spanning a subspace of low curvature U m U_{m} (defined in more detail below).
ℰ m ​ ( x ′ ) = ‖ U m ⊤ ​ g θ ⋆ ​ ( x ′ ) ‖ 2 \mathcal{E}_{m}(x^{\prime})=\|U_{m}^{\top}g_{\theta^{\star}}(x^{\prime})\|_{2} (1)

Here, we show that this score is proportional to the standard deviation of predictions across a local ensemble of models with near-identical training loss, and demonstrate that this approximation holds in practice.

Our derivation proceeds in two steps. First, we define a local ensemble of models with similar training loss, then we state the relationship between our underspecification score and the variability of predictions within this ensemble.
The spectral decomposition of the Hessian H θ ⋆ H_{\theta^{\star}} plays a key role in our derivation. Let
H θ ⋆ = U ​ Λ ​ U ⊤ , H_{\theta^{\star}}=U\Lambda U^{\top}, (2)

where U U is a square matrix whose columns are the orthonormal eigenvectors of H θ ⋆ H_{\theta^{\star}} , written ( ξ ( 1 ) , ⋯ , ξ ( p ) ) (\xi_{(1)},\cdots,\xi_{(p)}) , and Λ \Lambda is a square, diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues of H θ ⋆ H_{\theta^{\star}} , written ( λ ( 1 ) , ⋯ , λ ( p ) ) (\lambda_{(1)},\cdots,\lambda_{(p)}) , along its diagonal. As a convention, we index the eigenvectors and eigenvalues in decreasing order of the eigenvalue magnitude.

To construct a local ensemble of loss-preserving models, we exploit the fact that eigenvectors with large corresponding eigenvalues represent directions of high curvature, whereas eigenvectors with small corresponding eigenvalues represent directions of low curvature. Thus, under the assumption that the model has been trained to a local minimum or saddle point, parameter perturbations in flat directions (those corresponding to small eigenvalues λ ( j ) \lambda_{(j)} ) do not change the training loss substantially (see Fig. 1 ). We characterize this subspace by the span of eigenvectors with corresponding small eigenvalues. Formally, let m m be the eigenvalue index such that the eigenvalues { λ ( j ) : j > m } , \{\lambda_{(j)}:j>m\}, are sufficiently small to be considered ‘‘flat’’. 1 1 1 For now, we take m m to be given, and discuss tradeoffs for choosing m m in practice in Section 3 . We call the subspace spanned by { ξ ( j ) : j ∈ σ } \{\xi_{(j)}:j\in\sigma\} the ensemble subspace . Parameter perturbations in the ensemble subspace generate an ensemble of models with near-identical training loss. 2 2 2 We note that not all loss-preserving ensembles will necessarily be local; however, the existence of some such local ensemble is sufficient to enable underdetermination.

Our goal is to characterize the variance of test predictions with respect to random parameter perturbations Δ θ \Delta_{\theta} that occur in the ensemble subspace. We now show that our underspecification score ℰ m ​ ( x ′ ) \mathcal{E}_{m}(x^{\prime}) is, to the first order, proportional to the standard deviation of predictions at a point x ′ x^{\prime} .

Finally, we note that we can obtain similar results for the standard deviation of the loss at test points if we redefine g g as the loss gradient rather than the prediction gradient.

We now discuss a practical method for computing our underspecification scores. The key operation is constructing the set of eigenvectors that span a suitably loss-preserving ensemble subspace (i.e. have sufficiently small corresponding eigenvalues). Because eigenvectors corresponding to large eigenvalues are easier to estimate, we construct this subspace by finding the top m m eigenvectors and defining the ensemble subspace as their orthogonal complement. Our method can be implemented with any algorithm that returns the top m m eigenvectors. See below for discussion on some tradeoffs in the choice of m m , as well as the algorithm we choose (the Lanczos iteration ( Lanczos, 1950 ) ).

Our method proceeds as follows. For a given choice of m m , we calculate the m m eigenvectors of H H with the largest eigenvalues. These eigenvectors define an m m -dimensional subspace which is the orthogonal complement to the ensemble subspace. We use these eigenvectors to construct a matrix that projects gradients into the ensemble subspace. Specifically, let U m ⟂ U_{m^{\perp}} be the matrix whose columns are these large-eigenvalue eigenvectors { ξ ( j ) : j ≤ m } \{\xi_{(j)}:j\leq m\} . Then U m ⟂ ​ U m ⟂ ⊤ U_{m^{\perp}}U_{m^{\perp}}^{\top} is the projection matrix that projects vectors into the “large eigenvalue” subspace, and I − U m ⟂ ​ U m ⟂ ⊤ I-U_{m^{\perp}}U_{m^{\perp}}^{\top} projects into its complement: the ensemble subspace. Now, for any test input x ′ x^{\prime} , we take the norm of this projected gradient to compute our score
ℰ m ​ ( x ′ ) = ‖ ( I − U m ⟂ ​ U m ⟂ ⊤ ) ​ g θ ⋆ ​ ( x ′ ) ‖ . \mathcal{E}_{m}(x^{\prime})=\left\|\left(I-U_{m^{\perp}}U_{m^{\perp}}^{\top}\right)g_{\theta^{\star}}(x^{\prime})\right\|.

The success of this approach depends on the eigenspectrum of the Hessian and the choice of m m . Specifically, the underspecification score ℰ m ​ ( x ′ ) \mathcal{E}_{m}(x^{\prime}) is the most sensitive to underdetermination in the region of the trained parameters if we set m m to be the smallest index for which the training loss is relatively flat in the implied ensemble subspace. If m m is set too low, the ensemble subspace will include well-constrained directions, and ℰ m ​ ( x ′ ) \mathcal{E}_{m}(x^{\prime}) will over-estimate the prediction’s sensitivity to loss-preserving perturbations. If m m is set too high, the ensemble subspace will omit some under-constrained directions, and ℰ m ​ ( x ′ ) \mathcal{E}_{m}(x^{\prime}) will be less sensitive. For models where all parameters are well-constrained by the training data, a suitable m m may not exist. This will usually not be the case for deep neural network models, which are known to have very ill-conditioned Hessians ( Sagun et al., 2017 , see, e.g., ) . It may be possible to develop diagnostics for choosing m m based on trace estimation techniques ( Hutchinson, 1990 ) or eigenvalue distributions ( Martin & Mahoney, 2018 ; Marčenko & Pastur, 1967 ; Wigner, 1967 ) , but we leave this as future work.

We use the Lanczos iteration to estimate the top m m eigenvectors, which presents a number of practical advantages for usage in our scenario. Firstly, it performs well under early stopping, returning good estimates of the top m m eigenvectors after m m iterations. Secondly, we can cache intermediate steps, meaning that computing the m + 1 m+1 -th eigenvector is fast once we have computed the first m m . Thirdly, it requires only implicit access to the Hessian through a function which applies matrix multiplication, meaning we can take advantage of efficient Hessian-vector product methods ( Pearlmutter, 1994 ) .

Finally, the Lanczos iteration is simple – it can be implemented in less than 20 lines of Python code (see Appendix B.1 ). It contains only one hyperparameter, the stopping value m m . Fortunately, tuning this parameter is efficient — given a maximum value M M , we can try many values m < M m<M at once, by estimating M M eigenvectors and then calculating ℰ m \mathcal{E}_{m} by using the first m m eigenvectors. The main constraint of our method is space rather than time — while estimating the first m m eigenvectors enables easy caching for later use, it may be difficult to work with these eigenvectors in memory as m m and model size p p increase. This tradeoff informed our choice of m m in this paper; we note in some cases that increasing m m further could have improved performance (see Appendix E ). This suggests that further work on techniques for mitigating this tradeoff, e.g. online learning of sparse representations ( Wang & Lu, 2016 ; Wang et al., 2012 ) , could improve the performance of our method. See Appendix B for more details on the Lanczos iteration.
